title: Fish fry setting and scrubbing steps with red brick
summary: Fish fries were mostly indoors in Prohibition days; the red brick and Gold Dust-style powder used to scrub steps are described.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Can you tell me a little bit more about the fish fries? Was that similar to a lawn party? Did they have them outdoors or in the house?

No, well, depending on how the weather was. But most of the fish fries that I had been to was more or less the inside. Inside? Yeah. You'd go over there and you'd buy fish and you could eat it there, you could even take it out. And of course that was during the prohibition days too, you could always buy a little home brew too. You know, and so I guess that's why some of the fellas used to come around there too, they'd get their little home brew and they'd drink their little wine and they'd have a boil until four or five o'clock in the morning. And the aroma was always so inviting, that's the thing I found so fascinating about it, to see the red larynx sitting on the outside and the red front. They used to pound the red brick a long time ago and they'd scrub the sidewalk with this red brick and when it dries off it made it nice and pretty. Well red color. Red color. Red color. Because you know a long time ago all the sidewalks were made with nothing but brick. It wasn't here until recently in the last few years that they started paving the streets, but most of the sidewalks was comprised of nothing but brick. And by the time, as a matter of fact when we were nothing but kids we used to sell red brick. Five and ten cents a bucket. That used to be. Powered it up. Powered it up.
That used to be our sideline.
Well we'd go to various lots, you know. Old houses had been torn down and we'd mass them in the wagon and roll them on the arm and pound it up. How'd you pound them up?
I'm going to try breaking one of them up.
Well with some kind of hard object or hammer or something like that. Yeah, anything.
It doesn't get gummy or anything. No.
Well it gets a little gummy because if you notice the red brick, it rains down there all the time. It was always raining. And the brick themselves, it stayed constantly damp.

That's what it was. So therefore it had a pretty good body to it. Yeah. It was cold and it stayed more or less together but very few times you would get it. It would be in such a powdered form that it would blow away. Yeah. You know. And even the humidity down there would help to keep it damp. Yeah. And they found out that it was a very good solution. They used to mix up grammer powder with this red brick and used to scrub the steps. What kind of powder?
It's a type of powder similar to the washing powders you have today. Oh yeah. But I remember that particular name because it was a popular brand there.
